newsitem.title: RWANDA: Stragglers, lost children shuffle into Rwanda.
newsitem.headline: Stragglers, lost children shuffle into Rwanda.

text.p: A ragged, exhausted host of hundreds of Hutu stragglers are shuffling in silence into Rwanda from eastern Zaire, escaping three weeks of fighting and gangs of marauding gunmen.

While Western nations debate whether a multinational force is needed to save lives, the stragglers say they left many more Rwandan refugees and displaced Zaireans hiding in forests and hills or being marched along by brutal troops and militiamen.

"We were hiding in the forest when the Interahamwe (a Hutu militia group) came and stole all we had, including all our food and shoes," said Jackson Twezeyimana, 31, who reached the Rwandan border town of Gisenyi on Friday.
"We came from Kahindo camp, where my brother was killed in the fighting three weeks ago. In the forest, there are still many, many people. We could see many camp fires when we left."

"Some are very afraid they won't get out alive. They think they will be killed by Interahamwe," he added. The Interahamwe are Rwandan Hutu militiamen who escaped to Zaire in 1994 and refuse to return because of their role in Rwanda's genocide.
Twezeyimana, his three boys aged 10, four and two, and his wife fled with only the dirty clothes on their backs and a pair of rubber boots he says the Banyamulenge Tutsi rebels gave him.

The stragglers, in contrast to most of the 500,000 Rwandan refugees to cross the border to Gisenyi in four days starting a week ago, are in poor shape, their feet swollen and their eyes vacant. Many are carrying nothing and plead for some food.
"It is dense forest so though it is the rains now we tried to drink sap from roots because there was no water," said Emmanuel Karimunda, 36, who trekked in with his wife and child.
"We hid in the forest but it was too dangerous so then we went into the hills, where we were all attacked," he added.

"There was shooting by soldiers, I don't know who they were. They shot into the mass of refugees and I saw between 80 and 100 killed at a place called Osso in the hills of Masisi district," he said. "We've walked and hidden for three weeks."

Aid officials say dangers for those still in Zaire include the Interahamwe and former Rwandan troops herding masses of refugees on forced marches to the north and west and bands of desperate, defeated Zairean troops hunting for food and loot.
In a Gisenyi school, seven-year-old Ebenezer Niziyimana sat on the concrete floor with tears running down his face, one of more than 4,000 children lost during the exodus from Zaire.

"I lost my sister on a road near Kahindo camp two weeks ago. There was pushing and she disappeared," said Niziyimana, covered with insect bites and wearing a torn shirt showing Donald Duck in a safari hat striding past tall palm trees.
"Disney in the Jungle," it said in English. Niziyimana told of how a Hutu woman found him wandering around after two days.
"The lady brought me over into Rwanda and left me here," said Niziyimana, adding he was looked after by a sister called Uwimana since his parents were killed fleeing to Zaire in 1994.
He said he was from the Gisenyi area. He will be kept at the school for lost children for at least 48 hours in the hope his elder sister or another family member will turn up for him.
Adrienne Cassidy, 28, of the agency Concern said 60 kids arrived at the centre near the border with Zaire on Thursday.
"Some of them are too young to even know their own names," she said. "They have boils, cuts and infected wounds and are in much worse shape than the ones we picked up nearly a week ago."
Aid workers on hearing that a mother accompanied by young children is dying at the nearby clinic on the border rushed there to glean any information at all on the family before she dies.
"It's essential if we stand any hope of finding relatives who might take in the children," said Cassidy, from Dublin.
"There is no joy in Rwanda because where are my parents," says Ephremu Niyitegeka, 14, wearing a man's black suit jacket too big for him. "To be back alone means I cannot enjoy this."
"I think they are still in the forest with my three sisters and two brothers. There was some shooting and they were gone."
